## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Explain the three parts of every ggplot: data, aesthetics and geoms.
2. Draw scatter plots, line charts, bar charts, histograms and box plots.
3. Map a variable to colour, and split a chart into panels with facets.
4. Add titles and axis labels, change scales and apply a theme.
5. Choose a chart type that fits your question.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(gapminder)
```

## The grammar of graphics

**ggplot2** builds a chart from layers. Every chart needs three things:

1. **Data**: a data frame.
2. **Aesthetics**: which columns go on which visual property, such as the x position, y position or colour. You set them inside `aes()`.
3. **Geoms**: the shapes that show the data, such as points, lines or bars. Each one is a `geom_` function.

You join the layers with `+`:

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()
```

Read it as: "take `penguins`, put flipper length on x and body mass on y, and draw points". The warning about removed rows is R telling you that two penguins have missing measurements.

::: {.callout-note}
## `+` not `|>`
ggplot2 is older than the pipe, so layers are joined with `+`. A common error is writing `|>` between layers. You can still pipe data **into** `ggplot()`: `penguins |> ggplot(aes(...))`.
:::

## Adding colour

Map a third variable to `colour` inside `aes()`, and ggplot2 adds a legend:

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

Now the chart shows something new: the three species form separate groups.

Setting a colour for **every** point is different. Put it outside `aes()`, as a fixed value:

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2, alpha = 0.6)
```

`alpha` sets transparency, which helps when points overlap.

## Common chart types

### Line chart: change over time

```{webr}
gapminder |>
  filter(country %in% c("Uganda", "Kenya", "Rwanda")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, colour = country)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

You can stack several geoms. Here, lines show the trend and points show each measurement.

### Bar chart: counts of categories

`geom_bar()` counts the rows for you:

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island)) +
  geom_bar()
```

If you have already calculated the values, use `geom_col()` and give it a y:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean_mass)) +
  geom_col()
```

### Histogram: the shape of one variable

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 200)
```

Try changing `binwidth`. Too wide hides detail, and too narrow shows noise.

### Box plot: compare a variable across groups

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

The box covers the middle half of the values, the line is the median, and dots are unusual values.

## Facets: small multiples

`facet_wrap()` draws one panel per group, with the same axes, so you can compare them easily:

```{webr}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ island)
```

## Labels, scales and themes

A chart for other people needs a title and clear axis labels. `labs()` sets them:

```{webr}
gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Richer countries tend to have longer life expectancy",
    subtitle = "Each point is a country in 2007. Point size shows population.",
    x        = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)",
    y        = "Life expectancy (years)",
    colour   = "Continent",
    size     = "Population",
    caption  = "Source: Gapminder"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

A few things are happening here:

- `scale_x_log10()` spreads out the crowded low-income countries. Use a log scale when values range over several orders of magnitude.
- A good title states the finding, not just the variables.
- `theme_minimal()` removes the grey background. Try `theme_bw()` or `theme_classic()` too.

## Choosing a chart

| Your question | Chart | Geom |
|---|---|---|
| How are two numbers related? | Scatter plot | `geom_point()` |
| How did something change over time? | Line chart | `geom_line()` |
| How many in each category? | Bar chart | `geom_bar()` or `geom_col()` |
| What does one variable's distribution look like? | Histogram | `geom_histogram()` |
| How does a number differ between groups? | Box plot | `geom_boxplot()` |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
In Excel you pick a chart type first, then the data. In ggplot2 you start from the data and the question, then add layers. Changing a bar chart into a box plot means changing one line, not rebuilding the chart.
:::

## Saving a chart

On your own computer, save the last chart you drew with `ggsave()`:

```r
ggsave("life-expectancy.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

## Exercises

In each exercise, save your chart as `p` and print it.

### Exercise 1: Scatter plot

Draw a scatter plot of `bill_length_mm` (x) against `bill_depth_mm` (y) for the penguins.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_scatter
#| setup: true
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)
aes_of <- function(p, a) {
  m <- p$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m) && length(p$layers)) m <- p$layers[[1]]$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m)) NA_character_ else rlang::as_label(m)
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_scatter
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = ______, y = ______)) +
  ______()
p
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex8_scatter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Put the column names inside `aes()`. Points are drawn with `geom_point()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex8_scatter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point()
p
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_scatter
#| check: true
if (!exists("p") || !inherits(p, "ggplot")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save your chart as p.")
} else if (!identical(aes_of(p, "x"), "bill_length_mm") || !identical(aes_of(p, "y"), "bill_depth_mm")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Put bill_length_mm on x and bill_depth_mm on y.")
} else if (!any(vapply(p$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint"), logical(1)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add geom_point() to draw points.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Across all penguins, longer bills seem to be shallower. Exercise 2 shows why that is misleading.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Map colour to a variable

Take the same chart and colour the points by `species`. What do you notice?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_colour
#| setup: true
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)
aes_of <- function(p, a) {
  m <- p$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m) && length(p$layers)) m <- p$layers[[1]]$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m)) NA_character_ else rlang::as_label(m)
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_colour
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, ______)) +
  geom_point()
p
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex8_colour"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Inside `aes()`, add `colour = ` followed by the column name.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex8_colour"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()
p
```
Within each species, longer bills are also deeper. Across all penguins together, the trend looked weak or even reversed. Colour revealed groups that hid the real pattern.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_colour
#| check: true
if (!exists("p") || !inherits(p, "ggplot")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save your chart as p.")
} else if (identical(aes_of(p, "colour"), "species")) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Within each species, longer bills are deeper.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Map colour to species inside aes(): colour = species.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Line chart

Draw a line chart of Uganda's life expectancy (`lifeExp`) over time (`year`). The data is already filtered for you as `uganda`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_line
#| setup: true
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(gapminder)
uganda <- gapminder |> filter(country == "Uganda")
aes_of <- function(p, a) {
  m <- p$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m) && length(p$layers)) m <- p$layers[[1]]$mapping[[a]]
  if (is.null(m)) NA_character_ else rlang::as_label(m)
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_line
p <- ggplot(uganda, aes(______)) +
  ______()
p
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex8_line"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Put `year` on x and `lifeExp` on y, then add `geom_line()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex8_line"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
p <- ggplot(uganda, aes(x = year, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_line()
p
```
Life expectancy rose until the late 1980s, fell during the 1990s, then recovered. A line chart makes that change easy to see.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_line
#| check: true
if (!exists("p") || !inherits(p, "ggplot")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save your chart as p.")
} else if (!identical(aes_of(p, "x"), "year") || !identical(aes_of(p, "y"), "lifeExp")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Put year on x and lifeExp on y.")
} else if (!any(vapply(p$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomLine"), logical(1)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use geom_line() to draw a line.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Notice the fall in the 1990s and the recovery after.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Labels

This box plot works, but it has no title and the axis labels are column names. Add a title and clear x and y labels with `labs()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_labs
#| setup: true
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_labs
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = ______,
    x     = ______,
    y     = ______
  )
p
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex8_labs"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Each label is text, so put it in quotes. A good title states the finding, for example `"Gentoo penguins are the heaviest"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex8_labs"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins are the heaviest",
    x     = "Species",
    y     = "Body mass (g)"
  )
p
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8_labs
#| check: true
has <- function(x) !is.null(x) && is.character(x) && nzchar(x)
labs_set <- if (exists("p") && inherits(p, "ggplot")) p$labels else NULL
if (is.null(labs_set)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save your chart as p.")
} else if (!has(labs_set$title)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add a title inside labs(), in quotes.")
} else if (!has(labs_set$x) || !has(labs_set$y) || identical(labs_set$y, "body_mass_g")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Give both axes clear labels, such as \"Species\" and \"Body mass (g)\".")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Your chart now explains itself.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using `|>` instead of `+` between layers.** ggplot2 layers are joined with `+`.
- **Putting `+` at the start of a line.** End each line with `+`. If the next line starts with `+`, R thinks the chart has already finished.
- **Fixed colours inside `aes()`.** `aes(colour = "blue")` creates a legend entry called "blue" in the default red. Put fixed values outside: `geom_point(colour = "blue")`.
- **`geom_bar()` with a y value.** `geom_bar()` counts rows. If you already have the values, use `geom_col()`.
- **Titles that only name the variables.** "Mass by species" says what is plotted. "Gentoo penguins are the heaviest" says what it means.

## Summary

- Every ggplot has data, aesthetics (`aes()`) and geoms, joined with `+`.
- Map variables to x, y, colour or size inside `aes()`. Set fixed values outside it.
- `geom_point()`, `geom_line()`, `geom_bar()`/`geom_col()`, `geom_histogram()` and `geom_boxplot()` cover most needs.
- `facet_wrap()` draws one panel per group.
- `labs()` sets titles and labels, `scale_*()` functions change axes and `theme_*()` functions change the look.
